As shown in Table 2 , Embedding Similarity and InfoMatch (Sent) achieve the highest N N scores (0.905 and 0.805), indicating that inter-model distances remain close to intra-model distances relative to the random-pair reference. In contrast, BLEU and ROUGE-L, which capture lexical overlap, exhibit substantially lower N N scores (0.341 and 0.505), revealing greater cross-model separation in wording. This distinction between semantic similarity and lexical differences is broadly consistent across question types (Figure 7 ). Models share broad linguistic and affective profiles. Beyond semantic correspondence, models exhibit substantial similarity in several grammatical, linguistic, and affective characteristics, including POS and dependency distributions, emotion profiles, and concreteness. Presentational conventions show more varied patterns: List Use exhibits moderate cross-model separation ( N = 0.700 N=0.700 ), whereas Markdown Emphasis Use shows much stronger separation ( N = 0.364 N=0.364 ). Models retain distinct lexical characteristics, structural patterns, and interactional conventions. Despite these shared characteristics, substantial cross-model differences remain in other aspects. For example, Lexical Diversity (MTLD; N = 0.332 N=0.332 ) exhibits strong separation, while Response Length ( N = 0.433 N=0.433 ) shows moderate separation. Interactional conventions are even more distinctive, with Opening and Closing Templates exhibiting the lowest N N scores among all metrics (0.115 and 0.101), indicating that their inter-model distances are much closer to the random-pair reference than to intra-model distances. 6 How Does LLM Homogeneity Evolve? Section 5 identifies three patterns of cross-model similarity: shared semantic content, common linguistic profiles, and distinctive response conventions. We next trace how these patterns evolve across generations from 2024 to 2026 (§ 6.1 ) and across post-training stages (§ 6.2 ). Because a change in N N can reflect either weaker inter-model homogeneity or stronger intra-model repetition, we analyze D inter D_{\mathrm{inter}} and D intra D_{\mathrm{intra}} separately throughout. 6.1 Across Model Generations We analyze fifteen open-weight models from the Gemma, Qwen, OLMo, GLM, and Granite families, with one release per family from each year between 2024 and 2026, using the same prompts and sampling configuration as in Section 5 . Newer models become more self-consistent, yet more distinct from one another along many metrics. From 2024 to 2026, intra-model distances change significantly for 22 of the 25 metrics, decreasing in 17 (77%). 4 4 4 a 2024–2026 change is considered significant if its 95% CI excludes zero, based on 10,000 prompt-level bootstrap resamples (prompts resampled jointly across models and years). This trend spans all five textual dimensions, extending the single-snapshot, embedding-based evidence of intra-model repetition reported by Jiang et al. (2025) . In contrast, inter-model distances change significantly for 21 metrics, increasing in 14 of them (67%). Notably, several metrics exhibit decreasing intra-model distances alongside increasing inter-model distances (Figure 3 ). Global semantic convergence masks growing inter-model differences. Consistent with prior work, embedding similarity suggests strong cross-model homogeneity both synchronically ( Wenger and Kenett, 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) and diachronically ( Patel et al., 2026 ) : it yields the highest normalized similarity among all 25 metrics ( N = 0.905 N=0.905 ; § 5 ), and inter-model embedding distance decreases by 10.0% from 2024 to 2026. However, this convergence is not reflected in finer-grained semantic measures: Sentence-level InfoMatch distance increases by 9.6%, while BLEU and ROUGE-L distances also increase. These contrasting trends suggest that embedding similarity alone may increasingly overstate inter-model homogeneity. Human-salient form features partly converge, while model-specific conventions diverge. Among the five metrics most strongly correlated with human form judgments (§ 4.1 ), three show decreasing inter-model distances: List Use ( − 39.8 % -39.8\% ), Paragraph Density ( − 22.3 % -22.3\% ), and List Density ( − 21.1 % -21.1\% ). However, the largest cross-generational divergences occur in lexical characteristics and interactional conventions, which correlate weakly with human form judgments (Table 3 ). For example, inter-model distances increase by 169.0% for Closing Template and 78.0% for Lexical Diversity. Together, models increasingly share how they organize responses, while becoming more distinct in their lexical and interactional conventions. 6.2 Across Post-Training Stages To understand how the three patterns of cross-model similarity identified in Section 5 evolve during post-training, we compare corresponding checkpoints from the OLMo 3 and Tülu 3 pipelines. 5 5 5 Because base models are elicited with few-shot demonstrations, we treat them as a reference rather than a directly comparable stage, and focus on changes among the post-trained checkpoints (SFT, DPO, and RLVR), which share the same generation setup. Experimental details are provided in Appendix D.3 . Semantic convergence continues beyond supervised fine-tuning. As observed in § 5 , current models share substantial semantic content, while Section 6.1 shows that global semantic similarity has increased across model generations. Tracing two post-training pipelines, we find that semantic convergence continues during preference optimization. Inter-model embedding distance decreases from 0.252 at SFT to 0.172 at DPO, with a smaller further reduction to 0.164 at RLVR. Sentence-level InfoMatch, BLEU, and ROUGE-L show consistent increases in cross-model similarity. Unlike the mixed generational trends, preference optimization reduces inter-model distances across all three semantic aspects: global semantic similarity, sentence-level correspondence, and lexical overlap. SFT introduces distinctive response patterns, while later stages reshape them unevenly. Sections 4 and 5 identify response organization and formatting conventions as important to human-perceived form similarity, alongside model-specific lexical characteristics and interactional conventions. Our stage-wise analysis shows that many of these differences become pronounced during SFT. Later stages, however, reshape these differences in different directions: by RLVR, Header and Opening/Closing Template mismatches increase further, while List Density differences decrease, and MTLD distance increases at DPO before declining at RLVR. Unlike a uniform diversity-collapse account of post-training, these findings reveal different trajectories across textual dimensions: preference optimization continues to increase semantic similarity while selectively amplifying or reducing model-specific differences in textual form. 7 Conclusion We revisit LLM homogeneity through a multidimensional lens, using 25 metrics across five textual dimensions to separate what models say from how they say it. Our human study shows that perceived similarity depends on both, whereas whole-response embeddings capture content only partially and form hardly at all. Viewed through this lens, LLM homogeneity emerges as a multidimensional and evolving phenomenon, where semantic convergence, structural alignment, and model-specific differentiation coexist. These patterns emerge at three levels of comparison. Across current models, LLMs say similar things in different words: they share global semantics and broad linguistic characteristics but retain distinct lexical characteristics, structural patterns, and interactional conventions. Across generations from 2024 to 2026, models have become more like themselves but not more like one another. Intra-model repetition increases for most metrics, while inter-model differences widen in fine-grained content, wording, and interactional conventions, even as global embedding similarity rises and several human-salient organizational features converge. Across post-training stages, these conventions emerge during SFT and are selectively reshaped, rather than uniformly collapsed, by preference optimization. These findings caution against relying on embedding similarity alone, which reduces homogeneity to a single convergent trend and obscures metrics that move in other directions. More broadly, evaluations of LLM homogeneity should distinguish content from form, and intra-model repetition from inter-model similarity, when tracing how responses evolve across generations and post-training stages. Limitations Language, prompts, and decoding. We focus on English open-ended prompts from Infinity-Chat , since open-ended generation is where homogeneity concerns are most pressing, and several of our metrics rely on linguistic resources well established mainly for English. We adopt the decoding configuration of Jiang et al. (2025) (temperature 1.0, top-p 0.9) to ensure comparability with prior work. Because temperature affects within-model variability, absolute distances may shift under other decoding settings. Extending the framework to other languages, task types, and decoding strategies is left for future work. Model coverage and confounds. Our cross-model analysis spans 18 models, yielding inter-model distances over 153 model pairs. For the generational analysis, few families offer open-weight releases in every year from 2024 to 2026, so model size and architecture are not held constant across releases. We therefore select the closest available sizes and evaluate hybrid-reasoning models in non-thinking mode for comparability. The resulting trends are descriptive and cannot be attributed to any single factor. We use lightweight API models because reliably estimating intra-model distances requires dozens of samples per prompt (at least 30 in our design), making larger proprietary systems costly to cover; such systems may exhibit different patterns. Normalized similarity. Raw metric values lack an absolute scale for how similar two responses are. Even for embedding similarity, the same score can mean different things under different embedding models. We therefore use random response pairs as an empirical upper bound on distance, which requires no metric-specific assumptions and places heterogeneous metrics on a common scale. However, because random pairs pool responses across prompts and models, this reference is not a strict bound for prompt-insensitive metrics. We therefore treat N N as a relative ranking and report raw distances alongside it. The analyses in Section 6 rely on raw distances rather than N N .
